hypotheses.title: Instrument normalized erasure (NE) as a first-class metric
hypotheses.description: Every experiment JSON already logs a timestamped event stream (asr_interim / translation_partial / translation_complete) with full text at each revision, but experiments/results.csv only ever tracks chrF/latency/glossary -- there is currently zero visibility into caption flicker/revision, which the survey identifies as one of the two things (with latency) that offline metrics completely miss. Compute character-level normalized erasure (per Arivazhagan et al.) retroactively over every existing experiment JSON's event stream, both for ASR interim text and for translation_partial text, and add it to results.csv going forward.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: No effect on the system itself (pure measurement); expected to reveal that translation-level NE is non-trivial today since interim ASR text is re-translated on every update with no masking/biasing.
hypotheses.required_changes: New analysis script under src/real_time_translation/experiments/ (or scripts/) that consumes the existing event log format; no changes to the live pipeline.
experiment_ids: retroactive: all experiments/*.json with a results.events list
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented src/real_time_translation/experiments/flicker_metrics.py (uv run real-time-translation-exp-flicker) and ran it over all 47 parseable experiment JSON files. Result: translation-level NE (char-level, per committed ASR window) is ~0.0001 -- essentially zero across the whole corpus, meaning the LLM-translation layer never rewrites already-shown text once a chunk commits (append-only streaming). ASR-level NE (word-level, per in-progress Deepgram interim hypothesis) is ~0.20 on average across 47 files (range roughly 0.01-0.32 per file) -- i.e. about 1/5 of the final word-length gets revised before the ASR hypothesis settles. This number independently matches a public description of NE found via WebSearch ('NE score of 0.2' = ~1/5 of tokens change before settling), which is a useful sanity check on the metric implementation. Conclusion: today's flicker risk lives entirely in the ASR interim layer, not in translation -- so h-masking-holdback and h-localagreement-asr-commit should be evaluated primarily on how much they reduce ASR-level NE (and, if TRANSLATE_INTERIM is ever turned on for live preview, whether that ASR instability leaks into translation-level NE, which it currently doesn't because translation only fires on committed windows). Caveat: NE formula was reconstructed from the survey's description, not verified against the Arivazhagan et al. primary source yet; the 4 oldest experiment JSON files (2026-04-xx) predate the current event-logging schema and were skipped (0 groups, not an error).

hypotheses.title: Hold-back masking on translation input to reduce flicker
hypotheses.description: Per Arivazhagan et al., truncate the last 1-3 words of the growing ASR hypothesis before sending to the LLM for re-translation (masking), instead of translating the full raw interim text every update. Compare NE, chrF, and end-to-end latency against the unmasked baseline on the same cached clip.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Lower normalized erasure (less visible rewriting) at the cost of a small latency increase (the last few words are deliberately withheld); chrF should be roughly neutral or slightly improved since the LLM sees less unstable trailing text.
hypotheses.required_changes: Add a hold-back-N-words step to the ASR-interim -> translation-input path (pipeline.py, near the existing masked_text low-confidence path at pipeline.py:381) gated by an env var so it can be A/B'd; add an experiment CLI flag to toggle it.

Code remains implemented and ready; still $0 spent.

hypotheses.title: LocalAgreement-2 gating before translation is triggered
hypotheses.description: Instead of sending every Deepgram interim update to the LLM, only trigger (re-)translation once two consecutive interim hypotheses agree on a longest-common-prefix (LocalAgreement-2, per whisper-streaming). Compare against baseline and against h-masking-holdback on NE/latency/chrF using the same cached clip. Explicitly scoped to plain text-level LocalAgreement-2, NOT an AlignAtt-style attention-based policy (see alignatt4llm-iwslt2026: that requires white-box access to the translating model's attention internals, which this repo's API-only Gemini/OpenAI translator does not expose) -- LocalAgreement-2 only needs externally observable ASR hypothesis text, which Deepgram already provides.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Fewer, more stable translation calls -> lower NE and possibly lower LLM cost per segment, at the cost of added latency while waiting for two-hypothesis agreement.
hypotheses.required_changes: New commit-gating layer between Deepgram interim callback and the translation queue in pipeline.py; needs its own toggle so it can run independently of h-masking-holdback.

hypotheses.title: Deepgram-bypass replay harness: test masking-holdback using only Gemini calls
hypotheses.description: This sandbox's network egress proxy blocks api.deepgram.com (confirmed 2026-09-08, see h-masking-holdback.blocked_reason) but NOT generativelanguage.googleapis.com -- so ASR-dependent live experiments (h-masking-holdback, h-localagreement-asr-commit) are stuck, but LLM-only ones are not. Every existing experiments/*.json already has a full `results.events` list (asr_interim/translation_partial/translation_complete, with is_utterance_end/text at each step -- the same schema src/real_time_translation/experiments/flicker_metrics.py already parses; CORRECTION cycle 4, 2026-09-08: this description originally also claimed utterance_id was a logged per-event field -- it is not. `TimedEvent` in video_segment.py has no utterance_id attribute and it is not present in the serialized JSON, only is_utterance_end is. Any utterance-span grouping over these events must use is_utterance_end boundaries as a sequential heuristic, not a true utterance_id join -- see h-cross-utterance-flicker, which needed this same fact and hit the same wrong assumption while scoping its required_changes). Build a small standalone script that replays a chosen experiment JSON's already-recorded ASR event stream (treating it as if it came from Deepgram live) through the same masking/batching/utterance-continuation logic as pipeline.py._translation_worker, but calling the real LLMTranslator directly instead of running the full TranslationPipeline+DeepgramTranscriber -- with/without masking_holdback_words toggled, on the same replayed ASR stream. This tests the real effect of h-masking-holdback on real Gemini output using zero new Deepgram spend and zero new Gemini spend beyond the replay's own translation calls (small, since it reuses already-transcribed text instead of re-running ASR).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Should reproduce (at lower cost, no Deepgram spend) the same NE/quality comparison h-masking-holdback was designed to measure, and unblocks progress on h-masking-holdback/h-localagreement-asr-commit even if api.deepgram.com stays blocked in future sessions.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script under src/real_time_translation/experiments/ (e.g. replay_masking.py) that: (1) loads an existing experiments/*.json's results.events, (2) reconstructs the per-utterance ASR text stream in order, (3) drives it through LLMTranslator with the same masking-holdback truncation logic as pipeline.py, (4) writes a normal experiments/YYYYMMDD_<name>.json + results.csv row so it's directly comparable via flicker_metrics.py. Needs care to faithfully reproduce _translation_worker's batching/utterance-lock semantics (pipeline.py:585-641) so the comparison is apples-to-apples with what a real run would do, not a simplified approximation.
hypotheses.note_cycle3: IMPORTANT design correction found while re-reading pipeline.py before attempting implementation (cycle 3, 2026-09-08): flicker_metrics.py's group_translation() groups translation_partial/translation_complete events by (asr_start_time, asr_end_time), which is the span of ONE batch/_stream_batch() call -- not the whole utterance. Per _stream_batch's own docstring, a continuation batch for an in-progress utterance 're-translates from scratch' (full_target_text, not incremental), so the interesting flicker h-masking-holdback is meant to reduce is the wording drift ACROSS a multi-batch utterance's successive from-scratch retranslations -- but that's currently invisible to flicker_metrics.py, which only measures within-one-call token streaming (always ~0 since streaming just appends tokens). This means: (1) h-flicker-metric's 'translation-level NE ~0' finding is real but doesn't actually rule out cross-continuation flicker -- it just wasn't measuring it, and (2) replay_masking.py (or a live h-masking-holdback run) needs a NEW across-batch comparison -- e.g. diffing each utterance's successive full_target_text retranslations directly -- not just reusing group_translation() as-is. Flagging for GENERATE_HYPOTHESES next cycle rather than expanding scope this cycle; see reflections.md cycle-3 entry.
hypotheses.blocked_reason: MAJOR FINDING cycle 5 (2026-09-09): attempted to implement replay_masking.py and hit a structural (not just complexity) blocker confirmed by reading pipeline.py's _translation_worker/_emit_batch_result and video_segment.py's TimedEvent/on_result closely. Masking-holdback only ever changes behavior on a CONTINUATION batch of a multi-batch utterance (pipeline.py: `if holdback > 0 and not is_last_of_utterance`) -- for a single-batch utterance, is_last_of_utterance is always True, so holdback is a guaranteed no-op. Testing the effect therefore REQUIRES per-batch NEW-fragment source (English ASR) text for continuation batches. But TimedEvent (video_segment.py, the only runner that logs `results.events` at all -- youtube_segment.py logs no per-batch events, only whole-utterance-final `results.segments`) stores only the TRANSLATED (Japanese) text per event, never the source text, for translation_partial/translation_complete events; the only source text recorded is the WHOLE utterance's cumulative text in `results.segments[].asr`, written once at utterance-end. So per-batch English source deltas for continuation batches are NOT recoverable from any of the 47 existing experiment JSONs -- this hypothesis's core premise ('replay a chosen EXISTING experiment JSON... zero new Deepgram spend') is infeasible as originally scoped, not just hard to implement carefully. Fixed the root data gap for FUTURE runs (small, $0, no API calls): added an `original_text` field to `TimedEvent` in video_segment.py, populated from `TranslationResult.original_text` at all 3 event-construction sites (asr_interim/translation_partial/translation_complete) -- see the commit history around 2026-09-09. Verified this doesn't break flicker_metrics.py (re-ran over all 47 existing JSONs, numbers unchanged: asr_ne_word_mean=0.2004, translation_ne_char_mean=0.0001, translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean=1.4430 -- matches cycle 4's ~1.47 finding) and passes `ruff check`. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this fix only helps a NEW recording made after this change -- it does NOT retroactively add the field to any of the 47 existing JSONs, all of which predate it (they have `original_text` absent, which the dataclass default ("") makes silently look like an empty string rather than erroring, so a naive future replay attempt against an OLD JSON would need to explicitly check for/reject empty original_text rather than assume it's just short text -- flagging this trap for whoever revisits this). Net effect: this hypothesis is no longer really a 'Deepgram-bypass' -- it still needs ONE new live Deepgram+Gemini recording (blocked by the same WS proxy issue as h-masking-holdback/h-localagreement-asr-commit, see their blocked_reason) to produce a JSON with original_text populated, before replay_masking.py itself (still not written) can be built and tested against it. Recommend GENERATE_HYPOTHESES either retire this as a separate hypothesis and fold it into h-masking-holdback directly (once live Deepgram access returns, just run h-masking-holdback for real -- no need for a separate bypass path anymore since the bypass premise is broken), or keep it open only as a way to validate the new logging itself once one live run happens for any reason.

hypotheses.title: Measure cross-continuation (across-batch) translation flicker, not just within-batch
hypotheses.description: Follow-up to h-flicker-metric's methodology gap, found and flagged in h-gemini-only-masking-replay.note_cycle3 (cycle 3, 2026-09-08): flicker_metrics.py's group_translation() groups translation_partial/translation_complete events by the (asr_start_time, asr_end_time) key of a single _stream_batch() call, so it only ever measures within-one-call token streaming (append-only, hence the ~0.0001 result h-flicker-metric reported). It cannot see the wording drift that matters for h-masking-holdback/h-localagreement-asr-commit: per _stream_batch's own docstring, each continuation batch for an in-progress, not-yet-committed utterance re-translates the full accumulated source text from scratch, so a later batch's full_target_text is not guaranteed to keep the same prefix as an earlier batch's -- that cross-batch rewriting is currently invisible. This hypothesis adds a second, across-batch grouping and NE computation over the same already-recorded event logs (retroactive, $0, no new Deepgram/LLM spend) to find out whether that invisible flicker is actually large or negligible.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect a materially higher NE than h-flicker-metric's within-batch ~0.0001 translation figure, since from-scratch retranslation across batches has no structural guarantee of prefix stability the way token-by-token streaming within one call does. If the across-batch NE turns out to also be small, that would be a genuinely useful negative result: it would mean h-masking-holdback/h-localagreement-asr-commit are optimizing a problem that mostly doesn't exist on the translation side (matching h-flicker-metric's conclusion that today's flicker risk lives in the ASR interim layer), and effort should stay focused on ASR-level NE instead.
hypotheses.required_changes: Add a new grouping function to src/real_time_translation/experiments/flicker_metrics.py, e.g. group_translation_by_utterance(events), that walks translation_partial/translation_complete events in file order and starts a new utterance-span group immediately after any event with is_utterance_end=True (the prior group's boundary). IMPORTANT: results.events/TimedEvent has no utterance_id field at all (verified cycle 4, 2026-09-08 by reading video_segment.py's TimedEvent dataclass and an actual experiment JSON -- only is_utterance_end is logged; the claim otherwise in h-gemini-only-masking-replay's original description was wrong and has been corrected there). So this grouping is a sequential is_utterance_end-boundary heuristic, valid for these single-speaker sequential-utterance experiments, not a true utterance_id join -- state this caveat explicitly in any report that cites the result. Within each utterance-span group, take the last (most complete) event's text per distinct (asr_start_time, asr_end_time) batch, in that order, and compute char-level normalized_erasure() (already implemented, reused as-is) over that ordered list of per-batch full texts -- this is the across-batch analogue of the existing within-batch group_translation(). Add the new column(s) (e.g. num_translation_utterance_spans, translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean) to flicker_metrics.csv's writer and to analyze_experiment()/FlickerReport, and print a corpus-wide mean alongside the existing two, exactly like h-flicker-metric did. No changes to the live pipeline; this only reruns the existing `uv run real-time-translation-exp-flicker` script over the same 47 experiment JSON files h-flicker-metric already used.
experiment_ids: retroactive: all experiments/*.json with a results.events list (via group_translation_by_utterance)
hypotheses.result_summary: Prediction confirmed, and more strongly than expected. Implemented group_translation_by_utterance() in flicker_metrics.py (sequential is_utterance_end-boundary heuristic, since results.events has no true utterance_id) and reran over all 47 experiment JSON files (275 utterance spans globally that involved >=2 _stream_batch() calls, out of 4471 total spans -- so about 6.2% of utterances take long enough to span multiple committed batches). Across those 275 multi-batch spans, mean cross-batch translation NE (char-level, computed the same way as h-flicker-metric's within-batch metric) is ~1.47 (median ~1.28 at the per-file level, range 0.68-3.94), vs. h-flicker-metric's within-batch translation NE of ~0.0001. An NE above 1.0 means the cumulative erasure across a span's successive full_target_text retranslations exceeds the length of the final translation -- i.e. when an utterance spans multiple batches, the LLM is not incrementally refining a prior Japanese translation, it is replacing nearly all of it each time (confirmed by manual inspection of experiments/20260903_smoketest.json's raw events: batch 1 for one utterance reads 'そして、私たちの主な仕事は、どのように読み解くかを理解することにあり、' and batch 2 for the SAME utterance reads 'その根底にある行列をどう読み解くかについてですが、ここでは詳しく触れずに、' -- unrelated wording, not a shared prefix). Conclusion: h-flicker-metric's 'translation flicker is negligible' finding was correct only for the ~94% of utterances that finish within a single batch; for the ~6% that don't, on-screen Japanese captions are being substantially rewritten mid-utterance, which is exactly the kind of viewer-visible flicker h-masking-holdback/h-localagreement-asr-commit are meant to reduce (both currently blocked on Deepgram infra, see their blocked_reason). This raises those hypotheses' priority once Deepgram access is restored, and suggests a cheap mitigation worth considering even sooner: suppressing/holding the display update for a continuation batch's full_target_text until it stabilizes, rather than rendering every batch's raw output. Caveat: span boundaries are a sequential heuristic (no true utterance_id), and the finding has not yet been cross-checked against wall-clock timing (how long, in seconds, an utterance needs to run before it crosses a second batch) -- a natural follow-up for a future cycle.
